Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimant, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, a Guatemalan citizen, is claiming refugee protection in Canada under section 96 and paragraph 97(1)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
The following is a summary of the claimant's allegations, as they appear in his Personal Information Form (PIF).
The claimant was a XXXX and his wife ran a small business out of the family home in XXXX XXXX.

In XXXX 2010, the Maras approached him on the road and ordered him to pay them, from that day forward, 1,000 quetzals a month, or else he and his family would be killed. His wife, who was at the family home, was issued the same demand at the same time in a note sent by the Mara 18.

The claimant and his family left the family home that day and sought refuge, by going into hiding, at the home of the claimant's brother-in-law in XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. The claimant's wife and their children still live there.
Fearing for his life, the claimant left Guatemala on XXXX XXXX, 2010, and arrived in Canada on December 6, 2010.
The claimant's identity was established to the panel's satisfaction by means of the exhibits submitted on record, in particular, the copy of his passport and his birth certificate.1
Given the evidence on record, the panel is of the opinion that the claimant did not establish that he fears persecution on one of the five Convention grounds.

The claimant fears a criminal gang, the Maras, for reasons related to money extortion. In the panel's opinion, there is no nexus between the grounds invoked by the claimant in support of his fear and one of the five Convention grounds as defined in section 96 of the IRPA. Consequently, this claim will not be analyzed under section 96 of the IRPA.
The claimant did not invoke a fear of torture to support his claim. Consequently, his refugee protection claim will not be analyzed under paragraph 97(1)(a).
The panel is of the opinion that the claimant gave testimony without contradictions and exaggerations. The claimant appeared credible to the panel.

After reviewing the documentary and testimonial evidence, the panel is of the opinion that the claimant would face a generalized risk should he return to Guatemala; he failed to establish that he would be subjected to a personalized risk based on personal circumstances, under paragraph 97(1)(b).

Paragraph 97(1)(b), under which the claimant is seeking protection, contains exceptions such that any person who alleges a fear of being subjected to a risk to their life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment must be subjected to it "in every part of that country"; moreover, the fear must not be "faced generally by other individuals in or from that country."2

In order for the claimant not to fall within this exception, he must satisfy the following criteria: he must be personally subjected to the risk, and the risk must not be generalized. In other words, the claimant's risk must be different from the risk that the Guatemalan population may face. Even if the claimant has already been a victim of violence in the past, his risk may be generalized.3

In Laurore Jean,4 the Honourable Justice Shore of the Federal Court stated that "[t]he case law of this Court is clear and consistent that a generalized fear of crime caused by a situation prevailing throughout the country and affecting the entire population is not enough to justify granting the status of person in need of protection." The panel informed the claimants' counsel that the generalized risk was the issue in the case.

In response to the question [translation] "Why were you targeted, why you?", the claimant responded that he did not know, that they had a store at the house, that he (the claimant) worked as a photographer, and that he and his wife could therefore be perceived as having money.

The claimant was asked whether other people in Guatemala could, like him, also be victims of extortion. The claimant responded yes. When asked whether his risk was different from that of these other people who, like the claimant, were victims of extortion from criminal gangs, the claimant responded that each person faces a different risk. Some are bombarded and others are forgotten.

When asked whether there was something in his story that rendered his risk different from that of other people who were extorted, the claimant responded that his risk would go on forever because there was a lot of corruption.

In light of the evidence on record, the panel is of the opinion that although the claimant may be personally subjected to a risk, that risk is no different from the risk faced by large subgroups of the population, such as storekeepers or people like the claimant who have a job and are perceived by the gangs as a source of illicit and quick profit.

The documentary evidence concerning this reveals that Guatemala has a nearly insurmountable crime problem. Citizens from all backgrounds are likely to be at risk of murder, kidnapping, extortion and killings between rival gangs.5 Violence from criminals toward the population appears to be generalized.

The issue of generalized risk is a principle that the case law confirmed in Prophète,6 in which the Honourable Justice Tremblay-Lamer states: "The risk of all forms of criminality is general and felt by all Haitians. While a specific number of individuals may be targeted more frequently because of their wealth, all Haitians are at risk of becoming the victims of violence."

In Paz Guifarro,7 Justice Crampton stated that a businessman who was beaten and robbed after refusing to pay a tax imposed by a criminal gang in Honduras and who filed a complaint to the police and was then beaten by the gang as a result of this complaint would face a generalized risk should he return to his country of origin.

In light of the evidence on record, the panel is of the opinion that the risk to which the claimant would be subjected is a generalized risk; it is the same risk to which the population, or at least those who are perceived as being able to provide criminals with a quick and illicit source of money, is subjected.
For these reasons, the panel concludes that the claimant's claim may not be allowed under paragraph 97(1)(b) of the IRPA.
The claimant failed to satisfactorily discharge his burden of establishing a serious possibility of persecution on one of the five Convention grounds.

He also failed to demonstrate that, should he return to Guatemala, he would be personally subjected to a danger of torture, to a risk to his life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.
For these reasons, the panel determines that XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX is not a "Convention refugee" or a "person in need of protection."

Consequently, his refugee protection claim is rejected.
